title: GHS Hazard Pictograms
summary: The nine standardized symbols used on chemical labels to show what kind of hazard a substance presents - the fastest way to size up a container before reading anything else on it.
quick_actions: Red-diamond border means a GHS hazard pictogram - stop and read it before handling, even if nothing else on the label is in a language you read.
Flame = flammable/self-heating/pyrophoric. Flame over circle = oxidizer (feeds fire even without its own flame source). Never assume these are the same hazard.
Exploding bomb = explosives, self-reactive substances, or organic peroxides. Gas cylinder = contents under pressure (can rupture or cause frostbite on release).
Corrosion = can destroy skin, eyes, or metal on contact. Skull and crossbones = can be fatal or seriously toxic in small amounts - treat as the most serious of the nine.

Health hazard = longer-term risk (carcinogen, respiratory sensitizer, organ toxicity). Exclamation mark = a milder acute hazard (irritant, skin sensitizer) - still worth PPE, just a lower tier than the skull symbol.
Environment (non-mandatory in the US) = harmful to aquatic life - relevant to disposal, not just handling.
more_info: A label can carry more than one pictogram at once - a solvent might show both the flame and the health-hazard symbol, and each one is a separate, additive warning rather than a summary. The absence of a pictogram is not the same as "safe": some hazard categories (certain irritants, some physical hazards) are not required to carry a pictogram at all. When in doubt, or when a label is unreadable, damaged, or missing entirely, treat the container as unknown/hazardous until its Safety Data Sheet can be found.

diagram.alt: The nine GHS hazard pictograms in a labeled 3x3 grid: Health Hazard, Flame, Exclamation Mark, Gas Cylinder, Corrosion, Exploding Bomb, Flame Over Circle, Environment, and Skull and Crossbones, each with its associated hazard categories listed underneath

title: Reading a Safety Data Sheet (SDS)
summary: Every hazardous chemical sold commercially is required to have a Safety Data Sheet - a standardized, 16-section document that says far more than the label ever could. Knowing the section layout means finding the one fact needed without reading the whole thing.
quick_actions: Sections 1-3: what it is (identification, manufacturer contact) and what's in it (hazard classification, ingredient composition).
Section 4 (First-Aid) and Section 5 (Fire-Fighting): what to do right now if something goes wrong - read these before an incident, not during one.
Section 6 (Accidental Release) and Section 7 (Handling and Storage): spill response and day-to-day safe-storage guidance specific to that substance.
Section 8 (Exposure Controls/PPE) says exactly what protective equipment and ventilation that specific chemical calls for - more specific and more reliable than a generic assumption.
Sections 9-11 (physical/chemical properties, stability/reactivity, toxicology) hold the technical detail; Sections 12-16 cover ecological, disposal, transport, and regulatory information.
No SDS on hand for something in use? That is itself a hazard-recognition red flag, not a minor paperwork gap - treat an unlabeled or undocumented chemical with real caution.
more_info: The 16-section format is a global standard (not just a US requirement), so an SDS for the same product looks the same shape whether it was issued in the US, the EU, or elsewhere - the section numbers and order do not change. This page explains the structure only; the actual hazard data for a specific chemical always lives in that chemical's own SDS or in a reference such as the NIOSH Pocket Guide below, never invented or assumed.

title: Exposure Limits and PPE Selection Logic
summary: Occupational exposure limits (like an OSHA PEL or NIOSH REL) describe how much of a substance in air is considered acceptable over a work shift - understanding the shape of that number matters more than memorizing any single value.
quick_actions: An exposure limit is not a line between "safe" and "dangerous" - it is a time-weighted average considered acceptable for a full workday, and short high-concentration exposures can still be hazardous well under that average.

"IDLH" (Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health) values, where listed, describe a level requiring immediate evacuation and the most protective respiratory equipment - a distinct, more urgent threshold than a routine exposure limit.

PPE selection follows the hazard, not habit: skin/eye contact calls for gloves/goggles matched to that specific chemical's compatibility (not all gloves resist all chemicals), while airborne exposure calls for ventilation first and respiratory protection second.

Odor is an unreliable warning system - some hazardous gases have strong odor thresholds well above dangerous concentrations, and some (like carbon monoxide) have none at all. Never use "I can't smell anything" as a safety check.
A reference such as the NIOSH Pocket Guide lists these figures per chemical - the value for one substance says nothing about a different one, even in the same general chemical family.
more_info: This page explains how to read exposure-limit and PPE information found in a chemical reference; it is not itself a source of exposure limits for any specific substance. Look up the actual chemical in the NIOSH Pocket Guide (or its SDS) rather than estimating from a similar-sounding one.

title: Recognizing Categories of Chemical Hazard
summary: Beyond the pictograms themselves, chemical hazards fall into a few broad families worth recognizing on sight: physical hazards (fire/reactivity), health hazards (toxicity), and environmental hazards - each calling for a different kind of caution.
quick_actions: Physical hazards are about the chemical itself reacting - flammability, explosivity, reactivity with water or air, or being an oxidizer. These are about what the substance can do to its surroundings.

Health hazards are about what the substance does to a person - acute toxicity (immediate effects at a given dose), corrosivity (skin/eye damage), sensitization (allergic-type reactions), and longer-term hazards like carcinogenicity.
A single substance can carry hazards from more than one family at once (see GHS Hazard Pictograms above) - a physical hazard and a health hazard are not alternatives, they stack.

"Incompatible" is a real, specific concept: different hazard classes stored or used together can react dangerously (a classic example is mixing an oxidizer with a flammable material) - always check a chemical's own SDS Section 7 for its specific storage/incompatibility guidance rather than assuming.
Unknown or unlabeled containers should be treated as hazardous by default until identified - this is standard practice, not overcaution.
more_info: This is a general orientation to hazard categories, not a substitute for consulting the SDS or label of an actual chemical in hand. Specific chemical compatibility and storage-segregation requirements vary by substance and by jurisdiction; treat anything here as a starting vocabulary, not a compatibility chart.

title: Basic Material Properties for Repair and Handling
summary: A handful of everyday material properties explain most of why one material is chosen over another for a repair or a container - hardness, strength, corrosion resistance, and flammability chief among them.
quick_actions: Hardness resists scratching/denting but says little about toughness - a hard material can still be brittle and crack under a sudden impact that a softer, tougher material would absorb.
Tensile strength is resistance to being pulled apart; compressive strength is resistance to being crushed - many materials (cast iron, concrete) are strong in one and weak in the other.

Corrosion resistance depends heavily on the environment, not just the material - stainless steel resists rust far better than plain steel in most conditions, but certain grades still corrode in high-chloride (salty/coastal) environments.

Flammability and heat tolerance matter for storage and repair choices alike - know whether a material or its stored fuel/solvent presents a fire hazard before applying heat, sparks, or an open flame nearby.

Dissimilar metals in direct contact with moisture present (e.g. aluminum against steel) can corrode faster than either would alone (galvanic corrosion) - worth knowing before joining or storing mixed-metal hardware outdoors.
more_info: These are general, widely-taught material-science concepts rather than data from one specific retained document - see Fastener Basics and Bearings & Lubrication on the Mechanical & Repair page for the fastener- and bearing-specific version of some of these same ideas.

title: General Safe Storage and Handling Principles
summary: A short set of general-purpose habits - not tied to any one chemical - that reduce risk across almost any hazardous-materials situation: labeling, segregation, ventilation, and never relying on memory.
quick_actions: Keep every container labeled - if a substance is ever transferred to a different container, copy the hazard information onto the new one immediately, not "later."
Store incompatible hazard classes apart (see Recognizing Categories of Chemical Hazard above) - proximity during a leak, fire, or spill is exactly when incompatibility matters most.
Work in ventilated areas when using anything with a pictogram or a noticeable odor, and don't rely on smell as a warning system (see Exposure Limits and PPE above).

Lock out/tag out equipment before servicing anything that could unexpectedly energize, pressurize, or move - the same discipline OSHA's electrical-hazard guidance describes applies broadly to mechanical and chemical hazards too.
Know the location of eyewash, first-aid, and fire-suppression resources before starting work with a hazardous material - not after something goes wrong.
more_info: This page intentionally stays at the level of general safe-handling habits rather than step-by-step procedures for any specific hazardous task - always follow the specific SDS, label, and any applicable local regulations for the actual substance or equipment in hand.

title: Chemical Storage Groups: Keeping Incompatibles Apart
summary: A lettered scheme (compatible organic/inorganic acids, bases, oxidizers, pyrophorics, and more) for grouping chemicals so incompatible ones never share a shelf, plus what to look for when inspecting a storage area.
quick_actions: Segregate by hazard class first, alphabetize within a group second - alphabetizing a whole shelf without grouping by compatibility first is a common, avoidable mistake.

Common storage groups: compatible organic/inorganic acids, compatible organic/inorganic bases, compatible oxidizers (including peroxides), and compatible pyrophoric/water-reactive materials are each kept apart from the others.

Secondary containment (a tray or bin under stored containers) should hold at least 10 percent of the total stored volume, or the volume of the largest single container, whichever is greater - so one failed container cannot spread into the rest.

Inspect stored chemicals periodically for container integrity (cracks, leaks, rust, illegible labels) and signs of degradation (crystals, clumping, discoloration, unusual odor) - a degrading container is a hazard on its own, separate from what is inside it.
A damaged or unidentified container is not something to open, move, or clean up alone - clear the area and get qualified help, the same default posture as an unknown spill.
more_info: This is a widely-used general storage-grouping concept, not a substitute for a specific chemical's own SDS Section 7 (Handling and Storage) - always follow the more specific guidance when the two ever seem to disagree.
